title: The Product Works In Demos But Not In Real Use
excerpt: A product can appear effective in demos while failing in real use when demo conditions do not match operational data, cognitive load, workflow patterns, or guidance needs. The failure is visible in post-sale adoption, support demand, and first unsupervised use.
metaDescription: Why products that work in controlled demos fail under real data, ambient cognitive load, developer-model workflows, and unassisted use.
summary: This situation describes the gap between controlled demo performance and operational performance. It covers data mismatch, cognitive load mismatch, developer model substitution, and guidance architecture mismatch, with grounded examples from Polymatica, Pixelart Fugo, Squaremind, Assemblio, and visioncheckout.
definition: A demo-to-real-use gap occurs when a product performs under controlled demonstration conditions but fails when users operate it independently with their own data, workload, environment, timing, and recovery needs.

bodyMarkdown:
## Demo performance and operational performance are different conditions

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

A product can work in demos and fail in real use because demo conditions and real working conditions are structurally different environments. In a demo, a product specialist controls the data, the scenario, the pace of the walkthrough, and the audience's frame of reference. In real use, none of those controls persist.

Users bring their own data into the product. That data may be incomplete, inconsistently structured, or inherited from previous systems. Users also operate under their own cognitive load, alongside other work, without a guide. They may return to the product after days away to check or change something rather than experiencing it as a fresh, linear walkthrough.

The result is a performance gap between what the product appears to communicate in the sales process and what it can consistently deliver in operational use. Sales cycles can succeed while post-sale adoption fails.

## Data mismatch creates first-contact failure

Data mismatch occurs when a product is developed, tested, trained, or demonstrated against clean and idealised data, then meets operational data that has different properties. Sample datasets may be structured for clarity, and edge cases may be excluded from testing. Users trained on that data build a mental model that fits the training material but not their own files.

In real use, users may import records from legacy systems, duplicate entries, inconsistent column naming, files where the expected three columns are actually eight with overlapping content, or structured data formats the interface has not been tested against. The interface then provides no path through the condition because the condition was absent from product testing and training.

This is not a training failure when the training accurately explains the operation but omits the operational condition in which the operation is attempted. The failure appears at the first independent encounter with real data.

## Cognitive load mismatch appears when the guide disappears

Cognitive load mismatch occurs when a product is designed for the instructed experience of a demo but used in the ambient conditions of normal work. A demo specialist directs attention, explains transitions, and maintains the audience's frame of reference. The product only needs to perform one selected scenario in sequence.

Real use is less controlled. A user may be managing other work, encountering the product without guidance, or returning under time pressure to perform a task only partly remembered. Products designed for the demo experience often front-load visual complexity and assume prior orientation. In the first unsupervised session, that assumption can fail.

This failure is especially visible when the product relies on the demonstrator to supply context that the interface itself does not provide. Once the user operates alone, the missing orientation becomes part of the product's behaviour.

## Developer model substitution makes internal logic look usable from inside the team

Developer model substitution occurs when a product team builds and iterates without sustained user research, and the interface gradually encodes the development team's understanding of the system rather than the user's understanding of the task. The mismatch is hard to see from inside the team because the team's mental model matches the interface.

The problem becomes visible when a user who does not share that mental model encounters the product. A sequence that feels logical to the team may reflect the system's internal object model rather than the user's question, decision point, or recovery path.

Developer model substitution is a structural cause of demo-to-real-use failure because internal walkthroughs can continue to succeed. The interface appears coherent when explained by the people who already understand it, but becomes difficult when used independently by people who do not.

## The commercial and organisational cost is lost adoption after the sale

The commercial cost of a demo-to-real-use gap is lost post-sale adoption. A prospect can see a compelling demo, sign a contract, and then encounter a product that does not behave as expected under real use. Support tickets can rise, renewal conversations can become difficult, and the product's reputation can diverge from the sales process.

The organisational cost is decision error inside the product team. Teams that cannot distinguish demo performance from operational performance may attribute failures to user error or training quality when the product was not tested against the conditions in which it would be used.

This matters because the corrective action differs. If the root cause is operational mismatch, more explanation of the demo scenario does not address the product behaviour that users encounter independently.

## Polymatica shows how clean training data can hide messy operational data

Polymatica had built a technically capable OLAP analytics engine. Trained users became productive analysts, but every customer required the founder to deliver training personally, and before redesign only 2% of users could complete key operations independently without consulting help documentation.

Sandbox Experiments surfaced a precise failure mode. Training had used clean, well-structured sample data. When users imported their own real data for the first time, the interface provided no path through the condition they encountered.

A representative case involved a user importing a spreadsheet while expecting three columns: city, sales, and staff. The file contained eight columns. Cities appeared in two of them, and no single column contained only cities. The user could not identify which column to use, had no framework for diagnosing or correcting the issue, and stopped.

The design response was a data preparation and preview step between importing data and beginning operations. Users could inspect a sample of actual values from their file, rename columns to match their mental model, and exclude fields that would add noise. After this step was introduced, the messy-data failure mode largely disappeared from support requests.

The measured outcome across two redesign releases was an increase in independent task completion from 2% before redesign to 40% after release 1 and 56% after release 2. The evidence basis was product analytics from the live system.

## Pixelart Fugo shows how a workflow can encode the developer's sequence rather than the user's question

Pixelart Fugo served media agencies and organisations managing screens across locations, with content ranging from advertising campaigns to wayfinding displays during live events. The existing system had a known NPS of 57%, and the playlist setup workflow appeared logical and complete in the development team's walkthrough.

In real use, the workflow did not hold. Users returned to check what was playing, managed campaigns across 40 locations, and adjusted schedules for specific screens. The playlist setup was a linear wizard based on the system's internal logic for creating a playlist object. To check or change something, users re-entered the wizard and navigated back to the relevant step.

Sandbox Experiments surfaced two common use cases that had been treated as minor: organisations managing multiple screens at a single location, and media agencies running a single campaign schedule across 20 or 40 locations simultaneously. These were operational realities that the interface had made harder because the development team's model of typical use had been built into the product logic.

The redesign replaced the wizard with an overview structure showing three dimensions: what content plays, where it plays, and when it plays. Dedicated mini-flows configured each dimension independently. The structure encoded the user's question rather than the system's internal object model.

NPS moved from 57% to 89%. The evidence basis was client-measured before and after: Pixelart Fugo surveyed all existing users, and the second measurement was taken approximately two months after the redesigned platform launched.

## Squaremind shows guidance architecture mismatch in autonomous physical use

In the documented Squaremind case, the product worked technically but failed in autonomous use. Squaremind had built a working dermatology scanning device: hardware functioned, a robot arm scanned, and software processed images. In improvised internal tests and demonstrations to two friendly dermatologists, the technical capability was visible.

The failure appeared when the founders tested the device with actual patients, unassisted. In client-reported background testing, 14 users attempted the process and only 2 completed it. Of the remaining 12, 8 got stuck within the first minute and 4 got stuck around the 3-minute mark.

The failure was not described as technical. The interface had been designed from the developer's model of the scanning sequence: a linear sequence of instructions displayed at each step. The patient experienced a different situation: a first-time, unassisted physical process, alone in a room with a moving robot arm, with no recovery path if anything went wrong.

Creative Navy conducted 4 unstructured field observation sessions in France. These sessions were deliberately not structured as measurement because the system was performing too poorly for systematic measurement to produce useful signal. The observation established that patients who became confused had nothing actionable to recover with.

The design response used the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework across every step of the scan flow. It managed the patient's mental model at each stage, prevented specific physical confusion events before they occurred, and provided structured recovery when they did. Patient confusion was treated as a designed state with its own interaction requirements.

Post-redesign ecological testing involved 29 users in London and Paris and was co-conducted with an independent dermatologist. It produced 27 independent completions. The 12 users who got stuck all recovered and completed the procedure. The pre-redesign completion rate of 2 in 14 became 27 in 29, with the pre-redesign rate based on client-reported background evidence and the post-redesign rate based on Creative Navy-recorded ecological testing.

## Assemblio shows a client-stated shop-floor mismatch, not Creative Navy-observed field evidence

In the documented Assemblio case, the Smart Viewer demonstrated in conditions that did not match the shop-floor context as Assemblio described it. The viewer was tuned for mouse navigation but was used where there was no mouse and often nowhere to put one. A dark theme demonstrated well, while the client stated that the shop floor needed a light theme because the environment was bright.

The interface complaints collected by the client reflected desk assumptions meeting standing use: a dark scheme hard to see in bright environments, instruction text far too small, touch operation very difficult, buttons too small to hit, hard to read on smaller displays, annotations obscuring the object, a parts list showing everything rather than the current step, and arrows not following animated components.

Creative Navy did not observe a shop floor in this engagement. Every statement about the working environment in this example is client-stated and must not be blended with field observations from any other engagement. No time-saving, error-rate, training, or adoption figure is established for Assemblio in this page.

## visioncheckout shows measured operational timing for the system being replaced

In the documented visioncheckout case, a three-second touchless checkout was observed in live operation at approximately 13 seconds at a chemical manufacturer's staff restaurant, approximately 11 seconds at an automotive supplier's canteen, and approximately 25 seconds at a public-facing leisure venue. The product, flow, and headline checkout concept were the same, but operational conditions differed from the demo premise.

Creative Navy conducted field research at six locations across three organisations over five days. The research observed 563 interactions with the system in live operation, measured transaction durations with a clock during observation, and included interviews with 34 users and 13 catering staff. This was a focused programme by one researcher over five days, not a longitudinal study.

The largest single component of lost time was guests looking for their card, a condition no demo contained. When an error occurred, it took one to four minutes to resolve, during which three to twelve people could not check out. The three-to-twelve figure is an observed consequence of a measured duration, not an independently counted figure.

The visioncheckout timings describe the system being replaced, not the redesign. The touchless interaction itself was working well and was not to be dramatically changed. The redesign was in development: nothing had shipped, nothing about the new designs had been tested, and no outcome of any kind can be claimed.

## Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses the gap through operational research

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

For demo-to-real-use gaps, Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses the problem through Sandbox Experiments. Two practices are central in the examples documented here: domain learning and user research against real operational conditions.

Domain learning means the design team becomes productive users of the system being redesigned. In the Polymatica engagement, the team ran the software against their own real data during the research phase rather than only reviewing sample data. The messy-data failure mode became visible because the team encountered it as users.

User research against real operational conditions surfaces use cases that the development team's model has not accounted for. In the Pixelart Fugo engagement, Sandbox Experiments identified the single-location multi-screen pattern and the shared-schedule-across-locations pattern by observing what users actually did.

The Squaremind engagement adds guidance architecture mismatch as a related mechanism. The product had been designed for the uninterrupted case in which a patient follows every instruction correctly. Operational reality involved a patient encountering an unfamiliar physical process alone for the first time. Addressing that condition required designing recovery paths, not only the ideal path.

## Evidence boundaries for this situation

The evidence on this page is drawn from specific documented engagements and should not be generalised as a guaranteed outcome. Polymatica and Pixelart Fugo include measured before-and-after figures, but their evidence bases differ: Polymatica uses live-system product analytics, while Pixelart Fugo is client-measured NPS before and after.

Squaremind combines client-reported background evidence before Creative Navy's involvement with Creative Navy-recorded ecological testing after redesign. The pre-redesign and post-redesign evidence bases are therefore not identical.

Assemblio operating-context material is client-stated. Creative Navy did not observe a shop floor for that example, and the page establishes no measured adoption, training, time-saving, or error-rate outcome for Assemblio.

visioncheckout field timings describe the existing system in live operation and must not be read as a result of redesign. The redesign had not shipped, had not been tested, and had no outcome claim.

## Related pages

Related situation pages include product adoption problems where specialist onboarding remains necessary, training burden remains high, research does not inform product decisions, abnormal conditions break the interface, and users cannot recover cleanly from errors. The documented Squaremind, Assemblio, and visioncheckout cases provide named examples for parts of the demo-to-real-use gap where matching case pages are available in this knowledge base.
